title: COMMIT
description: Learn when COMMIT completes a transaction, preserve atomic transfer boundaries, handle uncertain responses, and distinguish savepoints, visibility and durability.

references.title: PostgreSQL SET CONSTRAINTS and deferred checking

questions.question_text: What does COMMIT do?
options: Successfully completes the transaction under its documented commit contract; visibility in other readers follows their isolation and snapshot rules
questions.explanation: Statement completion is not commit completion. Confirmed commit establishes the supported database outcome without forcing every existing snapshot to refresh.

questions.question_text: Under InnoDB READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ, can an ordinary consistent read in another transaction consume the writer’s uncommitted replacement values?
options: No; it uses an appropriate committed version, while locking reads can have different waiting behavior
Only if isolation is disabled entirely
Only SELECT statements can see uncommitted changes
questions.explanation: The stated levels prevent dirty reads. READ UNCOMMITTED can permit them, so isolation must be named rather than labeled proper.

questions.question_text: Can a transaction be undone after COMMIT has completed?
options: No — once committed, changes are permanent; correcting them requires a new, separate transaction
Yes, but only within the same session
questions.explanation: COMMIT is a one-way, irreversible boundary — ROLLBACK cannot undo an already-committed transaction.

questions.question_text: Can COMMIT fail, and how should deferred-constraint examples be scoped across engines?
options: Yes; for example PostgreSQL can reject a deferred constraint at commit, while InnoDB does not support that deferred foreign-key mechanism
Only network failures can cause COMMIT to fail
COMMIT failures are impossible in SQL databases
questions.explanation: Commit failure must be handled, but PostgreSQL deferred constraints must not be presented as InnoDB deferred foreign-key support.

questions.question_text: Under autocommit mode, when does an explicit COMMIT become meaningful?
options: Only once you've explicitly opened a multi-statement transaction with START TRANSACTION, overriding the per-statement autocommit behavior
Autocommit and explicit COMMIT cannot coexist in any database
questions.explanation: Explicitly starting a transaction is what makes a later explicit COMMIT meaningful, distinct from autocommit's implicit per-statement commits.

questions.question_text: Why does ROLLBACK not reverse MyISAM table writes as it can reverse pending InnoDB changes?
options: MyISAM doesn't support SQL at all
MyISAM is nontransactional, so its writes do not participate in InnoDB-style transaction rollback
COMMIT is disabled entirely on MyISAM
questions.explanation: This is an engine capability distinction, not evidence that the course judge or any hosted provider was verified.

questions.question_text: Which ACID property concerns persistence of committed changes within the documented settings and failure contract?
options: Durability, with guarantees bounded by the actual persistence settings, storage and failure scope
None of the ACID properties relate to COMMIT
questions.explanation: A successful live commit does not prove survival of every disaster or replace backup and restore verification.

questions.question_text: In the two-account transfer example, what happens to the debit and credit updates once COMMIT succeeds?
options: They become committed under the documented persistence contract; fresh eligible reads can observe them while existing snapshots may retain older versions
questions.explanation: Both supported changes commit together; other readers’ visibility still follows their isolation and snapshot rules.

questions.question_text: Does the final UPDATE returning prove COMMIT succeeded?
options: Only with a short table name
questions.explanation: Statement completion and transaction completion are different milestones.

questions.question_text: A destination UPDATE affects zero rows. What must the full workflow do?
options: Check the missing required effect and choose its failure path
Always commit because no exception occurred
questions.explanation: SQL success does not prove the required entity existed.

questions.question_text: Can an established REPEATABLE READ snapshot retain older values after another commit?
questions.explanation: Visibility follows each reader’s transaction observation context.

questions.question_text: What does a lost commit response establish?
questions.explanation: The server may have committed even if its response was lost.

questions.question_text: What should precede repeating an uncertain effect?
options: A new random identity every retry
Authorized reconciliation using a stable request identity
questions.explanation: Reconciliation distinguishes an existing completion from a new attempt.

questions.question_text: Does a duplicate-key error alone prove the same authorized payload succeeded?
questions.explanation: Ownership and semantic equivalence still need verification.

questions.question_text: Does creating a savepoint commit earlier work?
questions.explanation: Earlier supported changes remain pending in the same transaction.

questions.question_text: What remains after the stated bin exercise from 10 and4?
questions.explanation: The extra decrement is undone, leaving only the intended transfer.

questions.question_text: Can a later ordinary ROLLBACK reverse an earlier confirmed COMMIT?
questions.explanation: Committed correction requires a new operation or separate reviewed recovery.

questions.question_text: Why must helpers coordinate transaction ownership?
options: A helper commit can unexpectedly close the caller’s boundary
Every helper has independent nested transactions
questions.explanation: The decision must match the complete business operation.

questions.question_text: Does SELECT after COMMIT prove crash durability?
options: Yes, every storage failure was tested
No, it is a live result check
questions.explanation: Failure recovery needs separate controlled evidence.

questions.question_text: Does database rollback undo an unrelated email?
questions.explanation: External effects need a coherent coordination or delivery protocol.

original_questions.explanation: COMMIT is the successful, permanent conclusion of a transaction.

original_questions.question_text: Before COMMIT runs, can other transactions see the changes made so far?
options: No — under proper isolation, other transactions still see the old values until COMMIT succeeds
Only if isolation is disabled entirely
Only SELECT statements can see uncommitted changes
original_questions.explanation: Isolation (22.7) keeps uncommitted changes invisible to other transactions until commit.

Yes, but only within the same session

original_questions.explanation: Some constraint checks are deferred to commit time in certain databases, so COMMIT failure is a real scenario to handle.

original_questions.question_text: Under autocommit mode, when does an explicit COMMIT become meaningful?
options: Only once you've explicitly opened a multi-statement transaction with START TRANSACTION, overriding the per-statement autocommit behavior

original_questions.question_text: On the SQL judge platform used in this course, why does COMMIT have no observable effect difference from ROLLBACK on a MyISAM table?
options: MyISAM doesn't support SQL at all
MyISAM is non-transactional, so statements are effectively auto-committed regardless of an explicit COMMIT or ROLLBACK
COMMIT is disabled entirely on MyISAM
original_questions.explanation: This is the platform-specific gotcha discovered while verifying this chapter's coding problems — ENGINE=InnoDB is required for real transactional behavior.

original_questions.question_text: What ACID property does COMMIT primarily activate for a transaction's changes?
options: Durability — the guarantee that committed changes survive subsequent crashes
None of the ACID properties relate to COMMIT
original_questions.explanation: The moment COMMIT succeeds, Durability's crash-survival guarantee applies to those changes.

original_questions.question_text: In the two-account transfer example, what happens to the debit and credit updates once COMMIT succeeds?
options: They remain private to the transaction forever
They become permanent and immediately visible to all other transactions
original_questions.explanation: COMMIT finalizes and publishes both updates as a single successful unit.

coding_problems.title: Commit a Fund Transfer
coding_problems.task: Transfer200 from account1 to account2 and COMMIT using the supplied known-valid two-account fixtures. Preserve the retained final checker. This arithmetic exercise does not establish production authorization, concurrency or missing-row handling.
coding_problems.solution_sql: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-200 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+200 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;
coding_problems.check_sql: SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.original_check_sql: SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;

original_problem.title: Commit a Fund Transfer
original_problem.description:
Write a transaction that transfers 200 from account id 1 to account id 2 and commits it. Debit account 1 by 200, credit account 2 by 200, then `COMMIT`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  balance INTEGER NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
```

**Sample data**:

```sql
INSERT INTO accounts (id, balance) VALUES (1, 1000), (2, 500);
```
original_problem.editorial: Reference: `START TRANSACTION; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 200 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 200 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;` — ENGINE=InnoDB is required for this platform's transaction support to actually apply.
original_problem.sql_check_sql: SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;

edge_cases: Both required account rows exist in these fixtures.
Missing rows and concurrency require separate production checks.
hints: Use one explicit transaction and commit after both changes.
coding_problems.explanation: The known-valid rows change by-200 and+200 within one explicit transaction; the retained checker shows both final balances.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Write START TRANSACTION, the two updates, and COMMIT.

coding_problems.title: Commit the intended bin transfer only
coding_problems.task: Move3 units from bin1 to bin2. Mark a savepoint, tentatively subtract1 extra from bin1, roll back that extra change, then COMMIT. Return bin_id, quantity ordered by bin_id. Both bins exist with sufficient source quantity in supplied fixtures.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE commit_bins(bin_id INT PRIMARY KEY,quantity INT NOT NULL) ENGINE=InnoDB;
coding_problems.solution_sql: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE commit_bins SET quantity=quantity-3 WHERE bin_id=1; UPDATE commit_bins SET quantity=quantity+3 WHERE bin_id=2; SAVEPOINT intended_transfer; UPDATE commit_bins SET quantity=quantity-1 WHERE bin_id=1; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT intended_transfer; COMMIT; SELECT bin_id,quantity FROM commit_bins ORDER BY bin_id;
hints: A savepoint does not commit earlier changes.
Roll back the extra decrement before final COMMIT.
coding_problems.explanation: The intended-3/+3 remains pending while the later-1 is undone; COMMIT completes the remaining transaction.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Use one transaction, a savepoint, partial rollback, and COMMIT.

notes:
## Close a transaction with a deliberate outcome

COMMIT successfully completes the current transaction under the database's documented commit contract. Supported changes become committed work rather than pending changes an ordinary ROLLBACK can undo. Finishing the final UPDATE is different from sending COMMIT, and sending COMMIT is different from receiving confirmation that it completed. A reliable workflow identifies which of these milestones it has actually reached before announcing success.

Consider transferring two hundred units from account one to account two. The debit and credit should succeed together. If each statement commits separately under autocommit, the debit can become permanent before the credit is attempted. An explicit transaction provides the intended database boundary, but it does not invent authorization, row-existence checks, sufficient source quantity or a policy for repeated requests. Those remain requirements of the trusted operation.

## Trace the retained two-account exercise

The synthetic InnoDB fixture starts account one at one thousand and account two at five hundred. It guarantees the two required rows for the arithmetic exercise. Subtract two hundred from the first, add two hundred to the second and commit. The retained final checker displays the account identifiers and balances in ascending identifier order.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-200 WHERE id=1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+200 WHERE id=2;
COMMIT;
SELECT id,balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
```

The result is account one with eight hundred and account two with seven hundred. The combined quantity remains fifteen hundred. For starting balances five thousand and two thousand, the result is forty-eight hundred and twenty-two hundred. These exact outputs test the requested arithmetic on valid fixtures; they do not establish concurrent correctness, application authorization or crash durability.

A missing destination demonstrates why the exercise is not a complete production transfer service. An UPDATE affecting zero rows can succeed without raising a SQL error. Blindly committing after such a statement can leave the debit without its required credit. A trusted implementation must inspect the required effects and choose rollback when the business operation was not completed, even if the SQL parser and engine accepted each statement.

## Keep visibility separate from commit completion

Committing makes changes available according to other transactions' observation rules. An already established InnoDB REPEATABLE READ snapshot can continue to display an earlier committed version after another transaction commits. A fresh eligible read can observe the completed new state. This difference does not mean that only half the writing transaction committed; the readers are using different visibility contexts.

Use independent connections for a visibility experiment. Let A make both changes and leave its transaction open. Let B read under an explicitly recorded isolation level and transaction boundary. After A commits, issue a fresh eligible B read and compare both balances. Record whether B retained an old snapshot rather than assuming that every SELECT automatically begins a new observation context.

## Bound durability by the actual persistence contract

InnoDB logging and recovery support survival of committed state, but exact guarantees depend on persistence settings, storage behavior and the failure scope. A relaxed configuration or loss of every storage copy can exceed the guarantee demonstrated by one ordinary successful commit. Backups, replication and restore drills address additional operational requirements; their existence and effectiveness need their own evidence.

A SELECT immediately after COMMIT is a live-server result check. It does not exercise power loss, restart, redo recovery or restoration from an independent backup. Likewise, a MariaDB fixture run is compatibility evidence for that engine, not proof of the exact MySQL version or hosted provider. Name both the environment and the property observed instead of promoting a narrow result into a universal reliability claim.

## Reconcile a lost commit response

A server can commit and then lose its connection before the acknowledgment reaches the client. A similar connection error can occur when the server did not commit. The client therefore has an unknown outcome until a trusted reconciliation path establishes the result. Missing confirmation is not proof of rollback, and a network exception is not permission to duplicate the business effect blindly.

A stable authorized request identity can help discover whether the intended operation already completed. Reconciliation must verify the owner and semantic payload of an existing result, not merely find an identifier with the same shape. A duplicate-key error alone does not prove that the same request succeeded. Retrying with a new random identity can also defeat deduplication and turn one intended transfer into two.

| Observation | Established fact | Remaining responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Last UPDATE returned | That statement completed | Check the business effect and commit |
| COMMIT confirmed | Database commit succeeded under its contract | Respond and coordinate later delivery |
| Commit response lost | Client lacks confirmation | Reconcile before repeating the effect |
| Later ROLLBACK | Current pending work may be undone | Earlier committed work remains committed |

## Make transaction ownership explicit

One coordinated layer should choose commit or rollback for the complete business operation. A helper that commits unexpectedly can close its caller's larger intended transaction. MySQL does not provide general independently nested transactions merely because one function calls another. Inspect the driver's API and the actual statements executed, including procedures or helpers that might end the current boundary.

Ordinary DDL can cause implicit commits in MySQL. Mixing a table-definition change into row updates and assuming that one ROLLBACK reverses the complete sequence is unsafe. Nontransactional tables also do not acquire transactional rollback merely because START TRANSACTION appears nearby. Verify the storage engines and statement semantics of all participants instead of treating the transaction keyword as a wrapper around every possible effect.

## Use savepoints without mistaking them for commits

A savepoint marks a rollback position inside an open transaction. ROLLBACK TO can discard later supported changes while retaining earlier pending work. It does not commit the earlier work or make it independently durable. A full later rollback can still undo the transaction's remaining pending changes; a successful final commit completes the work still present.

The intermediate exercise transfers three units between bins, marks a savepoint, makes an extra tentative source decrement, rolls back that extra decrement and commits the intended transfer. Starting from ten and four, the final quantities are seven and seven. The temporary extra decrement must not survive. Starting instead from twenty and two produces seventeen and five, preserving the same intended three-unit movement.

This exercise tests savepoint placement and the final committed arithmetic. A result-only judge cannot prove that another connection observed the correct blocking behavior or that a machine failure preserves the outcome. Trace the pending state after each statement, then identify the exact additional experiment needed for each broader claim. A savepoint is useful precisely because it changes rollback scope without creating another independent transaction.

## Resolve errors and connection state explicitly

Errors before COMMIT can have statement or transaction scope. A constraint error can reject one statement while earlier changes remain pending; an InnoDB deadlock victim can lose the complete transaction. Use documented failure handling and explicitly resolve an unsuccessful attempt. A failed rollback attempt does not establish a clean connection, and an unusable connection must not be returned to a pool with unresolved transactional work.

Keep the transaction limited to the work that needs its locks and atomic boundary. Slow remote calls can prolong contention without becoming part of database rollback. An email, file write or external charge is not automatically undone by ROLLBACK. A reviewed outbox or another coordination design can connect database state with later delivery, but it has its own retry, deduplication and monitoring responsibilities.

## Solve the boundary challenges

For the beginner task, run the retained arithmetic transfer against both supplied starting fixtures and check the final combined quantity. Then explain the missing-destination counterexample and the trusted check needed to reject that unsuccessful business attempt. Keep the fixed-fixture exercise and the full production workflow requirements distinct so a simple teaching solution is not misrepresented as a complete transfer service.

For the intermediate task, trace the three-unit movement, savepoint, extra decrement, partial rollback and final commit. Explain which changes remain pending after the partial rollback and why the final COMMIT closes the intended work. Finally describe a lost acknowledgment without inferring either server outcome. Continue with [savepoints](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/savepoint), [autocommit](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/autocommit) and [durability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/durability) for the surrounding contracts.

diagrams.description: Updates remain pending until commit. A savepoint only marks a rollback position. A lost acknowledgment leaves client uncertainty requiring reconciliation.
